planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the last frost once soil has warmed thoroughly; Atlas is a vigorous long-vined butternut bred to size up beyond standard Waltham-type fruit, so give hills extra room and a full season to finish.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills after the danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest two plants per hill. Atlas is a large-fruited butternut hybrid that regularly produces tan-skinned squash well above the size of standard butternut types, with dense, deep orange flesh and a small seed cavity that gives a high usable-flesh ratio for roasting, soup, and processing. The long vines need a full, warm season and ample spacing to support the bigger fruit load, and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit sizing. Harvest once the rind has hardened to a uniform tan and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage to concentrate sweetness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Black Forest Squash (Compact Dark-Skinned Kabocha-Type Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm; Black Forest grows on a more restrained, semi-bush vine than full-sized kabocha types, making it a reasonable choice where garden space is limited.

directions: Direct sow seed in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, spacing plants to allow the semi-compact vines to spread without crowding. Black Forest bears small, deeply ribbed, near-black fruit with dense, dry, deep orange flesh and a sweet, nutty flavor reminiscent of kabocha, and its more restrained vine habit lets it fit into gardens too small for sprawling maxima types. Each plant sets several two- to three-pound fruits that store well once cured. Harvest when the rind has hardened and the stem has begun to dry and cork, then cure in a warm location for one to two weeks to deepen the sweetness before moving squash to cool, dry storage.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the last frost once soil has warmed; Table Treat vines are productive and benefit from full-season warmth to set multiple fruit per plant.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills after the last frost, thinning to the strongest two seedlings per hill. Table Treat is a vining acorn squash that sets a generous number of dark green, deeply ribbed fruit per plant, each with dry, sweet, pale orange flesh typical of the acorn type and a convenient single-serving size. The productive habit makes it a reliable choice for gardeners who want multiple small squash rather than fewer large ones. Harvest once the rind has dulled from glossy to matte green and resists a fingernail, then cure briefly in a warm spot before moving to cool storage; acorn types keep for a shorter period than hubbard or butternut squash, so plan to use them within a couple of months.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after the last frost once soil is warm; Snack Jack needs a full season for both the fruit and the hull-less seed inside it to mature fully.

directions: Direct sow seed in hills after frost danger passes, giving the sprawling vines ample room to spread. Snack Jack is grown chiefly for its naked, hull-less seeds, which lack the tough outer shell of standard pumpkin seeds and can be roasted straight from the fruit without hulling, while the medium orange fruit itself is sound enough for carving or cooking. Allow fruit to fully mature and the rind to harden before harvest, since immature fruit yields underdeveloped, less flavorful seed. Scoop seeds out promptly after harvest, rinse away the clinging pulp, and dry thoroughly before roasting or storing to prevent mold.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Soldacki is a tall, potato-leaf indeterminate that needs sturdy staking or caging to support its heavy pink beefsteak fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil once the weather has warmed, staking or caging plants early. Soldacki is a Polish heirloom beefsteak with distinctive potato-leaf foliage and smooth, rosy-pink fruit often exceeding a pound, carrying a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of the best pink heirlooms. The vigorous indeterminate vines keep producing over a long season and tend to hold up reasonably well under variable summer weather. Pick fruit when fully colored but still firm at the shoulders, and watch for cracking after heavy rain on a dry spell.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Indian Stripe shares the dark-shouldered coloring and potato-leaf foliage common to the Cherokee Purple family of heirlooms.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost risk passes, bracing plants with a sturdy cage. Indian Stripe produces potato-leaf vines and dusky purple-pink beefsteak fruit with darker, almost black-green shoulders, part of the same dark-fruited heirloom lineage as Cherokee Purple, with a deep, smoky-sweet flavor favored by collectors of purple and black tomatoes. Because the unusual coloring makes ripeness hard to judge by color alone, check for a slight give at the blossom end before picking. Fruit is best used fresh, since the thinner skin and soft texture of dark-fruited heirlooms don't hold up as well to long storage.

common_name: Brandywine OTV Tomato (Original Terra Cotta Strain)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; OTV is a potato-leaf Brandywine type that sets fruit somewhat more reliably than the classic pink strain in variable weather.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared soil once nights have warmed, staking firmly to support the heavy crop. Brandywine OTV is an orange-fruited sport of the classic pink Brandywine, keeping the same potato-leaf foliage and rich, old-fashioned tomato flavor but in a warm terra-cotta orange color with slightly earlier, more dependable fruit set. Fruit commonly runs a pound or more, with a meaty interior and relatively few seeds. Harvest at full color and handle gently, since the soft-fleshed fruit bruises easily and is best enjoyed fresh rather than stored.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Peacevine is a vigorous, early-bearing indeterminate cherry tomato suited to a sturdy cage or trellis.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, providing a tall cage or trellis for support. Peacevine is an open-pollinated red cherry tomato bred for home and market gardeners, setting heavy clusters of small, sweet, well-flavored fruit over a long harvest season on vigorous indeterminate vines. It tends to begin bearing earlier than many other cherry types and continues steadily through summer with regular picking. Harvest fruit at full color for the best sweetness, and pick frequently to keep the vines setting new clusters.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Zogola is an indeterminate pink slicer that benefits from staking or caging like other mid-season heirloom tomatoes.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once the weather has settled, staking vines as they grow. Zogola is a Polish heirloom producing smooth, round, rosy-pink fruit of a practical slicing size with a sweet, mild flavor typical of Eastern European pink tomatoes. The indeterminate vines are productive over a long season and tend to set fruit reliably in a range of summer conditions. Pick at full color and use promptly, since pink-fruited heirlooms generally have thinner skin and softer flesh than modern red hybrids.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Old Brooks is a vigorous, drought-tolerant indeterminate heirloom suited to a sturdy cage or stake.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained soil after frost risk has passed, staking or caging the vigorous vines. Old Brooks is an old American heirloom slicing tomato noted among seed savers for holding up well in hot, dry conditions where many modern varieties falter, producing medium to large red fruit with a solid, meaty interior and good old-fashioned tomato flavor. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and generally need only routine staking and watering to perform well through a full season. Harvest at full color and keep plants evenly watered to reduce blossom-end rot during dry stretches.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; like other green-when-ripe tomatoes, Malachite Box needs a gentle squeeze test rather than color alone to judge ripeness.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights have warmed, staking the indeterminate vines for support. Malachite Box is a Russian heirloom named for the deep jade-green color of its ripe skin and flesh, producing medium to large round fruit with a mild, sweet flavor and little of the acidity associated with unripe green tomatoes. Because the fruit never turns red, judge ripeness by a slight softening and a shift from bright to a duller, warmer green rather than by color change alone. Handle ripe fruit gently, since it softens readily, and use promptly once picked.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Black Zebra is an indeterminate striped tomato related to Green Zebra and benefits from similar staking and spacing.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, staking or caging to support the vines. Black Zebra produces small, round fruit striped in dark purple-brown over a deep green-gold background, a striking relative of Green Zebra with a richer, more complex sweet-tart flavor than its green counterpart. The compact, productive vines set fruit in good quantity over the season and make an attractive mixed-color addition to a salad or market display. Pick when the stripes have fully darkened and the fruit gives slightly to pressure, and use fresh for the best flavor and color impact.

common_name: Earl of Edgecombe Tomato (New Zealand Heirloom Orange Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this New Zealand heirloom is a tall indeterminate that needs sturdy staking to carry its large orange fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once the weather has warmed, staking vines firmly as fruit loads increase. Earl of Edgecombe is a New Zealand heirloom beefsteak prized for its large, smooth, deep orange fruit and mild, sweet, low-acid flavor, traits that have made it a favorite among gardeners who find red heirlooms too tart. The indeterminate vines are productive over a long season given consistent moisture and feeding. Harvest at full orange color and handle carefully, since large-fruited heirlooms are prone to cracking after uneven watering.

common_name: Wes Tomato (West Virginia Heirloom Pink Beefsteak)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Wes is a potato-leaf indeterminate heirloom that needs a sturdy cage or stake to carry its large pink fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil after frost risk passes, staking plants early to support the heavy fruit. Wes is a potato-leaf heirloom out of West Virginia producing large, smooth, rosy-pink beefsteak fruit with the rich, well-rounded flavor characteristic of the best Appalachian pink tomatoes. The vigorous indeterminate vines crop steadily through a long season with routine staking and watering. Harvest when fully colored but still firm, and water evenly during fruit development to limit cracking and blossom-end rot.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Dagma's Perfection is a tall indeterminate bicolor beefsteak that needs sturdy staking to support its large marbled fruit.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once nights have warmed, staking firmly to support the large fruit. Dagma's Perfection produces big, smooth beefsteak tomatoes marbled in yellow and red both inside and out, with a sweet, low-acid flavor typical of the bicolor heirloom class alongside varieties like Big Rainbow and Marvel Stripe. The indeterminate vines are productive given consistent moisture and feeding through the season. Harvest once the marbled coloring is fully developed and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, and water evenly to help prevent cracking on the large fruit.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Pink Accordion sets deeply ribbed, hollow-chambered fruit and benefits from sturdy staking like other large French-type heirlooms.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, staking vines to support the oddly shaped fruit. Pink Accordion bears dramatically ribbed, pleated pink fruit in the French coeur de boeuf tradition, with meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor well suited to slicing and stuffing. The deep folds of the fruit give it an almost sculptural appearance that sets it apart on a market table or in a mixed heirloom display. Harvest at full color and inspect the folds for hidden moisture that can encourage rot in humid weather, since the deep ribbing can trap water after rain.
